players.product: US utility - transformer buyer (HICO America customer)

quarterly_data.signal: Full-year 2025 operating earnings of $3.42 per share ($3.33 excluding RNG 45Z credits), both above the guidance midpoint; GAAP earnings $3.45 per share; estimated Moody's CFO pre-working-capital to debt nearly 100 basis points above the downgrade threshold. 2026 operating EPS guidance excluding RNG 45Z credit income is $3.40-$3.60 (midpoint $3.50, a 6.1% increase over the comparable 2025 guidance midpoint of $3.30) despite a Millstone double outage year, driven by continued strength in sales and higher regulated investment; total operating EPS guidance midpoint $3.57. Long-term 5% to 7% operating EPS growth reaffirmed, now expected in the upper half of the range starting in 2028.
quarterly_data.figure: 2025 operating EPS $3.42 per share; 2026 guidance between $3.40 and $3.60 per share, midpoint $3.50 (6.1% increase); upper half of the 5% to 7% growth rate range starting in 2028

quarterly_data.signal: Electric demand growth: in 2025 weather-normal sales in the Dominion Energy Virginia LSE increased 5.4%, and all of the top 20 peak demand days in the Dominion Zone occurred in the last fourteen months; management cites these as tangible data points of an accelerating, real-time demand trend (whose drivers include its data center pipeline) that requires incremental investment across the system to keep it reliable.
quarterly_data.figure: weather-normal sales increased 5.4% in 2025; all of the top 20 peak demand days in the last fourteen months

quarterly_data.signal: Data center pipeline: over 48 gigawatts in various stages of contracting as of December 2025 versus around 47 gigawatts as of September, an increase of approximately 1.4 gigawatts or 3% (split into substation engineering letters of authorization, construction letters of authorization and electrical service agreements). The demand forecast is validated by 20-plus gigawatts of signed ESA and CLOA contracts, and forecasted data center demand through 2045 is more than covered by existing signed ESAs and CLOAs (nothing is forecast from SELOAs). The vast majority of demand growth is driven by steady and consistent batches of cloud and inference data center modules, limiting reliance on any single project or customer. Starting in January 2027, large load customers with demand of 25 megawatts or greater face minimum demand charges, and new ESAs carry firm contract terms with exit fees and enhanced collateral. Virginia data center load has grown at a 20% CAGR since 2016 while residential rates averaged 9% below the national average. Other large customers are not being crowded out, and on a Virginia Senate proposal that could remove a data center tax benefit, management said the outcome is hard to predict but it expects data center growth to continue.
quarterly_data.figure: over 48 gigawatts in contracting stages as of December 2025 (around 47 gigawatts as of September; approximately 1.4 gigawatts or 3% increase); 20-plus gigawatts of signed ESA and CLOA contracts; data center load 20% CAGR since 2016

quarterly_data.signal: Five-year total capital estimate raised from $50 billion to approximately $65 billion, a 30% increase; over 90% of the increase is at Dominion Energy Virginia, 'home to the largest data center market in the world'; nearly two-thirds of the updated spend is eligible for rider recovery (subject to regulatory approval); investment base CAGR updated to approximately 10%. Growth spans electric transmission and distribution, with a notable increase in generation. Management continues to see additional investment across the value chain, biased towards the early 2030s and beyond, that is not yet in the plan. There is no capital for an SMR in this five-year plan (nuclear technology evaluation is still in its final stages).
quarterly_data.figure: from $50 billion to approximately $65 billion, representing a 30% increase; over 90% at Dominion Energy Virginia; investment base CAGR approximately 10%

quarterly_data.signal: Gas generation in the capital plan includes two CTs and three CCGTs, and Dominion has secured turbine slots for each project; the CCGT projects have projected in-service dates of 2032 through 2034. On November 25 the Virginia SCC approved the certificate of public convenience and necessity and rider for the Chesterfield Energy Reliability Center, an approximately one-gigawatt gas-fired facility expected to cost approximately $1.5 billion and enter service in 2029 (a petition for reconsideration was denied on February 12). Gas generation converts to cash slowly at first, and the projects deliver full cash flow once they enter service in the early 2030s.
quarterly_data.figure: turbine slots secured for two CTs and three CCGTs; CCGT in-service dates of 2032 through 2034; Chesterfield approximately one-gigawatt, approximately $1.5 billion, in service in 2029

quarterly_data.signal: On February 13 PJM announced its final selections in the latest transmission open window process, awarding Dominion a portfolio of projects totaling over $5 billion with in-service dates through 2032, the largest proposed investment by Dominion Energy Virginia since PJM began its open window process; much of it is in the updated capital plan, and some extends beyond 2030.
quarterly_data.figure: over $5 billion of PJM open window transmission projects; in-service dates through 2032

quarterly_data.signal: Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind is over 70% complete and on track to deliver first power to the grid by March: all 176 monopiles were installed faster than expected, the third and final offshore substation is installed, and deepwater export cables are in; around 70% of towers and nacelles and 30% of blades are fabricated; the first turbine was completed in January. The budget is $11.5 billion, including unused contingency of $155 million, and covers weather-delay contingency through July 2027; each additional quarter beyond that would add between $150 million and $200 million, part of it allocated to the financing partner (Stonepeak, under existing contractual provisions). Most turbines are expected in 2026 and some in 2027, at about 2.25 days per installation, and the rider assumes 50% deliverability until PJM network upgrades are done. Management calls CVOW the fastest way to bring significant low-cost electricity to customers 'who are leading the AI race'.
quarterly_data.figure: over 70% complete; budget $11.5 billion including unused contingency of $155 million; between $150 million and $200 million per additional quarter; 2.25 days per installation; 50% deliverability assumed

quarterly_data.signal: Millstone nuclear supplies over 90% of Connecticut's carbon-free electricity. 55% of its output is under a fixed-price contract through late 2029 (the PPA expires in August '29), the remainder is derisked by hedging, and its 2025 capacity factor was over 91%. Connecticut DEEP issued a zero-carbon energy RFP in January (bids due in March, evaluation coordinated with other New England states), with clarity on the outcome expected towards the back half of the year. Dominion is still evaluating support for incremental data center activity at Millstone, which it says must be pursued collaboratively with Connecticut stakeholders.
quarterly_data.figure: 55% of output under fixed-price contract through late 2029; capacity factor of over 91% in 2025

quarterly_data.signal: Financing the five-year plan: nearly 60% of investing cash flows and dividends comes from internal operating cash flow, about 10% from net hybrid issuance, 10% or so from common equity through the DRIP and ATM programs, and roughly 20% from long- and short-term debt. Equity issuance averages roughly 2.5% of market cap annually; about a third of the five-year equity falls in 2026-2028 and about two-thirds in 2029-2030, when the largest capital increases (particularly gas generation spend) occur.
quarterly_data.figure: nearly 60% internal operating cash flows; about 10% net hybrid issuance; 10% or so common equity; roughly 20% debt; roughly 2.5% of market cap annually
